variants.title: Run the experiment
variants.context: A chaos experiment measures normal behavior, states a falsifiable hypothesis, defines an abort boundary stricter than the hypothesis boundary, then injects a bounded fault, observes, removes it, and verifies recovery.
variants.prompt: A team wants to test replica loss. Put the experiment in order.

items.text: Inject the bounded fault, compare control and experiment, remove it, verify recovery.
Define the abort boundary, stricter than the hypothesis boundary.
Measure normal behavior: customer-facing output, traffic shape, release, topology, alerts.
State the hypothesis: fault, target, expected steady-state boundary, recovery behavior.

variants.hint: The abort boundary is defined before anything breaks.
variants.explanation: Baseline → hypothesis → guardrail → evidence. An outage without a hypothesis is not chaos engineering.

variants.title: Run the experiment
variants.context: A chaos experiment measures normal behavior, states a falsifiable hypothesis, defines an abort boundary stricter than the hypothesis boundary, then injects a bounded fault, observes, removes it, and verifies recovery.
variants.prompt: Dependency latency injection is planned. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Predict that success stays above the boundary under 300 ms added latency.
Set the automatic stop threshold on customer impact.
Inject, observe, remove, and prove recovery before declaring completion.
Record baseline p95 latency and success over a representative window.

variants.hint: Recovery proof is part of the run, not an afterthought.
variants.explanation: Verify queues, replicas, and side effects returned to normal after cleanup.

variants.title: Run the experiment
variants.context: A chaos experiment measures normal behavior, states a falsifiable hypothesis, defines an abort boundary stricter than the hypothesis boundary, then injects a bounded fault, observes, removes it, and verifies recovery.
variants.prompt: A zone-loss game day. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Remove the zone within the envelope, compare, restore, verify.
Define the abort condition and automatic stop.
Baseline the customer outputs and current topology.
Hypothesize that checkout stays above 99% with one zone gone.

variants.hint: Start from a claim about observable behavior, not a tool action.
variants.explanation: A falsifiable hypothesis turns a scary action into evidence.

variants.title: Write the hypothesis
variants.context: “Terminate a pod” is a fault. “Checkout success stays at or above 99% when one replica disappears” is a hypothesis. Steady state is a customer or system output, not component health.
variants.prompt: Which of these is a hypothesis rather than a fault?
options: Terminate one checkout pod during peak hours.
Add 200 ms of latency to every database call.
Checkout success stays above 99% with one replica gone.
optionFeedback: That is the fault action.
That is also a fault action.
It names the fault, target, boundary, and expected behavior in a falsifiable form.
variants.hint: Which statement can evidence prove wrong?
variants.explanation: A useful experiment begins with a claim about observable behavior.

variants.title: Write the hypothesis
variants.context: “Terminate a pod” is a fault. “Checkout success stays at or above 99% when one replica disappears” is a hypothesis. Steady state is a customer or system output, not component health.
variants.prompt: A team defines steady state as “all pods Running”. What is wrong?
options: It should track Ready pods rather than Running ones.
Steady state should be a customer or system output.
Nothing; running pods are what users depend on.
optionFeedback: Both are component states.
Component health supports diagnosis; it is not the hypothesis.
Users depend on successful checkouts, which running pods do not guarantee.
variants.explanation: Define normal behavior with an output, not a component.

variants.title: Write the hypothesis
variants.context: “Terminate a pod” is a fault. “Checkout success stays at or above 99% when one replica disappears” is a hypothesis. Steady state is a customer or system output, not component health.
variants.prompt: During a run the abort boundary is crossed and there is no automatic or dependable manual stop. Which outcome is this?
options: A held hypothesis, since nothing visibly broke.
An illegitimate outcome: the envelope failed.
A falsified hypothesis, caught by the boundary.
optionFeedback: The run passed the boundary with no way to stop, so nothing was demonstrated.
Crossing the abort boundary without a stop is not an experiment result; it is an incident.
Falsification happens inside the envelope.
variants.explanation: Held, falsified within the envelope, or aborted by the guardrail; never unbounded.

variants.title: Bound the risk
variants.context: Keep fault authority narrower than application authority: target only onboarded resources, grant only needed fault actions, use automatic stop conditions, make cleanup idempotent, keep an owner and manual stop available.
variants.prompt: The experiment identity can terminate any instance in the account. What should change?
options: Scope the identity to onboarded, tagged resources.
Nothing; broad authority is what makes the test real.
Run it only at night when traffic is low.
optionFeedback: Fault authority must be narrower than application authority.
Broad authority is how experiments become outages.
A quiet window shrinks the blast radius in time, not in scope.
variants.hint: What could this identity break by mistake?
variants.explanation: Preview resolved targets before a run when the platform supports it.

variants.title: Bound the risk
variants.context: Keep fault authority narrower than application authority: target only onboarded resources, grant only needed fault actions, use automatic stop conditions, make cleanup idempotent, keep an owner and manual stop available.
variants.prompt: An operator will watch a dashboard and stop the fault if things look bad. Is that sufficient?
options: Yes, an alert page will reach the operator.
Yes, if two operators watch in rotation.
No. Automatic stop conditions bound the run.
optionFeedback: A page still leaves minutes of damage before anyone can react.
More watchers do not automate the stop.
Automatic stops act faster than people.
variants.hint: How quickly must the fault stop?
variants.explanation: AWS FIS stop conditions use alarms to halt experiments automatically.

variants.title: Bound the risk
variants.context: Keep fault authority narrower than application authority: target only onboarded resources, grant only needed fault actions, use automatic stop conditions, make cleanup idempotent, keep an owner and manual stop available.
variants.prompt: After the run, the injected latency rule is still in place because cleanup failed halfway. What was missing?
options: Idempotent cleanup that verifies the restored state.
A longer experiment window for cleanup to finish.
A second fault to force the rule to expire.
optionFeedback: Cleanup must be repeatable and verified.
Cleanup failed partway; more time does not complete a half-applied undo.
Adding faults compounds it.
variants.hint: How do you know the fault is gone?
variants.explanation: Recovery proof is part of the contract.

variants.title: Size the blast radius
variants.context: Blast radius is the maximum traffic, tenants, instances, or failure domains exposed. The hypothesis boundary distinguishes held from falsified; the abort boundary stops the fault to protect users.
variants.prompt: Forty instances run in one zone. The experiment may affect at most 10% of them. How many instances are eligible?
variants.hint: Apply the percentage to the fleet.
variants.explanation: 10% of 40 is 4 instances. Preview the resolved targets before running.

mistakes.feedback: The blast radius bounds the fleet, not the whole of it.

variants.title: Size the blast radius
variants.context: Blast radius is the maximum traffic, tenants, instances, or failure domains exposed. The hypothesis boundary distinguishes held from falsified; the abort boundary stops the fault to protect users.
variants.prompt: The hypothesis boundary is 99% checkout success; the abort boundary is 97%. How many percentage points of margin separate them?
variants.hint: Subtract the abort boundary from the hypothesis boundary.
variants.explanation: 99 − 97 = 2 points. The abort boundary protects users; the hypothesis boundary decides held or falsified.

variants.title: Size the blast radius
variants.context: Blast radius is the maximum traffic, tenants, instances, or failure domains exposed. The hypothesis boundary distinguishes held from falsified; the abort boundary stops the fault to protect users.
variants.prompt: The injection window is 10 minutes at 500 requests per second. How many requests are exposed to the fault?
variants.explanation: 500 × 600 = 300,000 requests inside the window. Duration is part of the blast radius.

variants.title: Contain the fault
variants.context: Timeouts limit waiting, retries need budgets and idempotency, breakers stop repeated calls, bulkheads isolate capacity, fallbacks preserve only designed degraded behavior; none makes stale or fabricated data correct.
variants.prompt: An injected slowdown in one dependency spreads until every worker is waiting. Which control was missing first?
options: A fallback response for the slow dependency.
More workers to absorb the extra waiting.
Timeouts that bound how long one attempt waits.
optionFeedback: A fallback without timeouts never triggers.
More workers just fill up with the same waiting calls.
Unbounded waiting occupies workers and amplifies a local fault.
variants.hint: What keeps a slow call from occupying a worker forever?
variants.explanation: Timeouts limit how long one attempt consumes a budget.

variants.title: Contain the fault
variants.context: Timeouts limit waiting, retries need budgets and idempotency, breakers stop repeated calls, bulkheads isolate capacity, fallbacks preserve only designed degraded behavior; none makes stale or fabricated data correct.
variants.prompt: A fallback serves cached prices that are hours old during a fault. Is the fallback correct?
options: Only if the product accepts that much staleness.
Yes; serving an old price beats an error page.
Yes, as long as the cached response is fast.
optionFeedback: A fallback preserves a specific designed degraded behavior.
Wrong data can be worse than an error.
A fast answer at the wrong price is still the wrong price.
variants.hint: What did the product promise about freshness?
variants.explanation: A fallback is a product contract.

variants.title: Contain the fault
variants.context: Timeouts limit waiting, retries need budgets and idempotency, breakers stop repeated calls, bulkheads isolate capacity, fallbacks preserve only designed degraded behavior; none makes stale or fabricated data correct.
variants.prompt: One tenant’s failing dependency consumes every shared connection. Which control isolates it?
options: A longer timeout so calls have room to finish.
A retry budget capping attempts per request.
A bulkhead reserving capacity per tenant.
optionFeedback: Longer waits worsen the drain.
Budgets bound retries, not capacity share.
Bulkheads keep one dependency from consuming every shared resource.
variants.explanation: Capacity reserve and failure-domain placement keep surviving paths able to absorb work.
